beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Grounded, and four candidates to measure
beats.got: nothing new, a lecture header

beats.trigger: Grounded means traceable to a specific file, number or quote in a source.
beats.got: Grounded means I can trace a claim to a source. It doesn't mean the claim is true.

beats.trigger: at 85% each come to about 20% end-to-end: one task in five correct, four in five with a defect, usually where you won't see it.
beats.got: A long agent workflow with no checks is mostly wrong even when each step is mostly right. My CFO would understand that.

beats.trigger: Compounding that destroys single-pass reliability builds loop reliability.
beats.got: Repeated test and fix rounds cut the error rate fast, if the detector actually works.

beats.trigger: Fluency is not evidence, and the model cannot tell you which parts of its output are grounded.
beats.got: Nothing new. Asking "are you sure?" doesn't verify anything, and the slide already said that.

beats.trigger: You don't know which detection method catches what matters on *your* output, on *your* strategic question.
beats.got: Don't trust a method someone recommends. Run several on my own material and measure.

beats.trigger: Four candidates that fail in different directions, so the scoreboard shows real spread:
beats.got: Four checks: invention, overreach, bad citations, contradicting evidence. Each catches a different kind of miss.

beats.trigger: Against the Mata v. Avianca pre-read, source triangulation caught an unsourced "small firm" descriptor and an unsupported "ten minutes" estimate.
beats.got: A law-firm example that isn't mine, so I skimmed it. The scorer part (precision, recall, coverage) was the useful bit.

beats.trigger: Grounded output names what it doesn't know. A grounded judge names what it can't catch.
beats.got: The judge file says what it can't catch, which is honest.

beats.trigger: Grounding is the discipline; fabrication is the failure: invented case law, invented medications, confident numbers nobody can source.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Two runs is a demo, not a measurement.
beats.got: Running the same prompt twice shows drift but proves nothing. It takes five to ten runs to mean something.

beats.trigger: The winner becomes a judge file you carry into Module 6.
beats.got: The output is a file I keep and reuse.

beats.trigger: Aim for roughly 10% fabrication or misrepresentation: enough wrongness for the detectors to have a job, not nonsense.
beats.got: I get the agent to write a briefing with deliberate lies in it so I can test the detectors. Odd, but it makes sense.

beats.trigger: Save it. **Don't open it yet.** Keep the main session blind until the extractor has turned the briefing into claims.

beats.trigger: Thirty is not statistical, but enough to start seeing the pattern.
beats.got: The agent pulls 30 claims out of the briefing. It's a small sample but fine for a first pass.

beats.trigger: Four helper agents run in parallel on the same claim pool, each with its own detection method and its own output file.

beats.trigger: It measures precision (of what the detector flagged, how much was ungrounded?), recall (of what the scorer adjudicated as ungrounded, how much did the detector catch?), and coverage (did the detector look at the claim pool?).
beats.got: I see which check actually catches what, with numbers on my own claims. One detector flagged something the others missed.

beats.trigger: The scoreboard IS the explanation. You can point at a row and say *this is why I'm keeping this one*.
beats.got: I can defend my choice of check by pointing at a row. I can say that to my CFO.

take_homes: Don't trust a check because someone recommends it. Run a few on my own output and score them. The scoreboard lets me defend the choice.
A long unchecked agent chain is mostly wrong even if every step is mostly right, so a check has to be built in.
The judge is a file that says what it catches and what it can't. I can reuse it on the pricing briefing and hand it to the team.

monday.move: Run the groundedness judge on the pilot-cohort pricing brief before it goes to the pricing working group, and flag claims that don't trace to a source.
monday.who: Me, then ask one team member to run the same file on their own brief
monday.when: Monday morning, before the brief goes out
monday.stop_condition: If the judge flags nothing, or only things I already knew, I drop it. If it flags real contradictions in the sources, the team adopts it.
monday.blocker: The team has no shared place for context files, so the judge file sits in my directory and everyone would keep their own copy.

misconception.why: I came in thinking good use means better prompts. Here the value was a measured, reusable judge file, and picking it came from a scoreboard rather than from prompt wording. I still believe prompts matter, but the saved file with stated limits feels like the bigger part.

one_line: It was useful once I saw the scoreboard and left with a judge file I can run next week. The lecture slides repeat themselves and the law-firm example isn't mine.
